lessonTitle: Polymers: Classes, Glass Transition and Selection

blocks.text: A polystyrene model-kit part is rigid and cracks if bent at 20 degrees C, a polyethylene bottle flexes freely at the same temperature, and a rubber band stretches several hundred percent. All three are polymers; the difference lies in how their chains are linked and where the glass transition sits relative to room temperature.

blocks.markdown: A polymer consists of very long chain molecules, with strong covalent bonds along each chain and weak secondary bonds between the chains. How the chains are arranged and linked determines whether the polymer is a thermoplastic, a thermoset or an elastomer, and how it responds to temperature.

rows: Linear or branched chains; secondary bonds between chains; may be amorphous or semi-crystalline
Softens and flows; hardens again on cooling
Does not melt; degrades or chars at high temperature
Long flexible chains with sparse cross-links, used above Tg
Does not melt; stays rubbery until degradation
blocks.caption: The three classes of polymer.

blocks.title: Glass transition temperature, $T_g$
blocks.text: The temperature range through which an amorphous polymer changes from a hard, glassy solid to a soft, rubbery or leathery material as chain segments gain the mobility to move. It is a property of the amorphous regions and depends on chain stiffness and the heating rate. Typical values: polystyrene about 100 degrees C, PMMA about 105 degrees C, polycarbonate about 150 degrees C, natural rubber about -70 degrees C.

blocks.markdown: **Modulus against temperature.** For an amorphous thermoplastic, the modulus-temperature curve has four regions. (1) *Glassy*: below $T_g$ the chains are frozen, the polymer is stiff (about 1 to 3 GPa) and brittle. (2) *Glass transition*: over a range of about 10 to 20 degrees C the modulus drops by roughly three orders of magnitude. (3) *Rubbery plateau*: above $T_g$ the polymer is soft and extensible, with modulus of order MPa, held together by entanglements or cross-links. (4) *Viscous flow*: for an uncross-linked polymer at still higher temperature, the entanglements slip and the polymer flows like a viscous liquid, which is the regime used for moulding. Cross-linked polymers skip region 4.

blocks.title: Stress at 1 percent strain in glassy and rubbery states
blocks.prompt: An amorphous polymer has $E=3.0$ GPa in the glassy state and $E=3.0$ MPa in the rubbery state. Estimate the stress needed for 1 percent strain in each state.

steps.text: Use Hooke's law for small strain, $\sigma=E\varepsilon$, with $\varepsilon=0.01$.

blocks.answer: 30 MPa against 0.03 MPa, a factor of 1000: the polymer is a thousand times less stiff above $T_g$.

blocks.markdown: **Choosing a polymer for a snap-fit.** A snap-fit joint is a cantilever hook that is deflected during assembly and then returns to its original position to latch. It needs a polymer with (i) high permissible strain (several percent), (ii) good toughness and fatigue resistance, (iii) enough stiffness to hold the latch, and (iv) low creep and a $T_g$ or melting temperature above the service temperature. For a constant-section rectangular cantilever of thickness $h$, length $L$ and end deflection $y$, the maximum strain at the root is

blocks.caption: Obtained from beam theory: the end load $P=3EIy/L^3$ gives root moment $PL$ and strain $PLh/(2EI)$; $h$, $y$, $L$ in the same length units.

blocks.title: Checking a snap-fit hook
blocks.prompt: A hook has $h=2.0$ mm and $L=20$ mm and is deflected $y=2.0$ mm. The candidate polymer has a permissible assembly strain of 3 percent (assumed). Is it acceptable?

steps.text: Compare with the permissible strain: 1.5 percent is half of 3 percent.

blocks.answer: The strain is 1.5 percent, within the 3 percent allowance, so the hook is acceptable with a safety factor of 2 on strain.

items: Tough semi-crystalline thermoplastics (polypropylene, nylon, acetal) are the usual snap-fit polymers.
Thermosets are generally too brittle for snap-fits, and elastomers too soft to latch.
Keep the service temperature well below $T_g$ for amorphous polymers, or below the melting temperature for semi-crystalline ones, and allow for creep and stress relaxation.
Fillers and fibres raise stiffness but reduce the permissible strain.

blocks.title: Where to look first
blocks.text: For a polymer, find out whether it is amorphous or semi-crystalline, find its $T_g$ (and melting point), and compare these with the service temperature. The classes then tell you if the material can be remelted, will creep, or snap.

points: Thermoplastics have no cross-links and can be remelted; thermosets have dense cross-links and do not melt; elastomers are lightly cross-linked and used above $T_g$.
Through the glass transition an amorphous polymer's modulus falls by about three orders of magnitude, from GPa to MPa.
A snap-fit polymer must tolerate a strain of several percent: $\varepsilon=3hy/(2L^2)$ must be below its permissible strain, which points to tough thermoplastics.

questions.stem: Which polymer class has a three-dimensional network of covalent cross-links, so that it does not melt on heating but eventually degrades or chars?

options.text: All polymers melt at a well-defined single temperature

distractorRationale.a: Correct: heavy cross-linking fixes the network, so it cannot flow.
distractorRationale.b: Thermoplastics have linear or branched chains with secondary bonds between them and soften and flow on heating.
distractorRationale.c: Elastomers are lightly cross-linked and also do not melt, but the heavy, rigid network described here is a thermoset.
distractorRationale.d: Amorphous polymers soften over a range, and thermosets do not melt at all.

questions.explanation: In a thermoset, covalent cross-links join the chains into a rigid network formed during curing, so heating cannot make the chains slide. At high temperature the network decomposes before it flows, which is why thermosets cannot be remelted or recycled by remoulding.

questions.stem: Which description fits an elastomer such as natural rubber at room temperature?

options.text: Lightly cross-linked chains, used above their glass transition, capable of large reversible elastic strain
Linear chains that flow readily when stressed
A crystalline ceramic with ionic bonds

questions.correctOptionText: Lightly cross-linked chains, used above their glass transition, capable of large reversible elastic strain

distractorRationale.a: Correct: coiled chains uncoil under load and return when it is removed.
distractorRationale.b: This describes a thermoset such as cured epoxy.
distractorRationale.c: This would give permanent deformation, as in a thermoplastic above its melting temperature.
distractorRationale.d: Elastomers are polymers with covalent chains and secondary bonds, not ionic crystals.

questions.explanation: Elastomers have long, flexible, coiled chains joined by a small number of cross-links, and their glass transition is below room temperature, so the chain segments are mobile. Under load the chains uncoil, and the cross-links make the strain recoverable.

questions.stem: Polystyrene, which has a glass transition temperature of about 100 degrees C, is in its rubbery state at room temperature.
questions.explanation: Room temperature (about 20 degrees C) is below the glass transition temperature of polystyrene, so it is in the glassy state: stiff and brittle. It becomes rubbery only above about 100 degrees C.

questions.stem: At 25 degrees C, which of these amorphous polymers (typical glass transition temperatures in brackets) is in the glassy state?

options.text: All of them are glassy at 25 degrees C

distractorRationale.a: Correct: 25 degrees C is far below its glass transition temperature.
distractorRationale.b: This is well above its glass transition temperature, so it is rubbery.
distractorRationale.c: This is also far above its Tg, and therefore rubbery.
distractorRationale.d: Only polymers with a Tg above 25 degrees C are glassy.

questions.explanation: A polymer is glassy when the temperature is below its glass transition temperature and rubbery or leathery above it. At 25 degrees C only the polymer whose Tg is above this value, PMMA, is glassy.

questions.stem: A cantilever snap-fit hook of rectangular section has thickness $h=1.5$ mm and length $L=15$ mm, and is deflected by $y=1.8$ mm during assembly. Using the maximum root strain for a constant-section cantilever, $\varepsilon=\dfrac{3hy}{2L^2}$, calculate the strain in percent.
questions.explanation: Substituting in consistent units (mm), $\varepsilon=3(1.5)(1.8)/(2\times15^2)=8.1/450=0.018$, i.e. 1.8 percent. This must be below the permissible strain of the chosen polymer, which is often only a few percent.

questions.stem: A snap-fit cantilever of thickness 2.0 mm and length 25 mm is to be made from a thermoplastic whose permissible assembly strain is taken as 3.0 percent. Using $\varepsilon=3hy/(2L^2)$, calculate the maximum permissible deflection $y$ in mm.
questions.explanation: Rearranging, $y=2\varepsilon L^2/(3h)=2(0.030)(25)^2/(3\times2.0)=37.5/6=6.25$ mm. A longer or thinner beam allows a larger deflection for the same strain limit.

questions.stem: An amorphous polymer has a modulus of 2.8 GPa below its glass transition temperature and 2.0 MPa in the rubbery plateau above it. By how many orders of magnitude does the modulus fall through the glass transition (the base-10 logarithm of the ratio)?
questions.explanation: The ratio is $2.8\times10^9/2.0\times10^6=1400$, and $\log_{10}1400=3.15$. This large drop, typically about three orders of magnitude, is why the glass transition temperature sets the upper service temperature for an amorphous thermoplastic.

questions.stem: A designer is choosing a polymer class for a snap-fit battery cover, which must be bent repeatedly, resist cracking and hold its shape. Which is the best choice and reason?

options.text: A tough semi-crystalline thermoplastic such as polypropylene or nylon, because it tolerates large elastic strains and repeated flexing
A highly cross-linked thermoset such as cured epoxy, because it is the stiffest
An elastomer such as silicone rubber, because it can stretch most
A glassy brittle thermoplastic such as unmodified polystyrene, because it is cheap

questions.correctOptionText: A tough semi-crystalline thermoplastic such as polypropylene or nylon, because it tolerates large elastic strains and repeated flexing

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it has a high strain capability and good fatigue life.
distractorRationale.b: Thermosets are brittle and cannot tolerate the strain needed for snap-fits.
distractorRationale.c: An elastomer is too compliant and would not hold its shape or provide a positive latch.
distractorRationale.d: Brittle polymers crack at the root of the snap-fit when deflected.

questions.explanation: A snap-fit needs a material that can take a few percent of strain repeatedly without cracking, retain stiffness for a positive latch, and resist creep. Tough thermoplastics such as polypropylene, nylon or acetal meet these requirements; brittle thermosets and glassy polymers do not, and elastomers are too soft.

questions.stem: Distinguish thermoplastics, thermosets and elastomers in terms of molecular structure, behaviour on heating and typical applications. Explain why only one of the three can be reprocessed by remelting.
markingGuide: Thermoplastics: linear or branched chains held by secondary bonds; soften and flow when heated; e.g. polyethylene, nylon (2 marks)
Thermosets: dense covalent cross-link network formed during curing; do not melt, degrade at high temperature; e.g. epoxy, phenolic (2 marks)
Elastomers: lightly cross-linked, flexible chains used above Tg; large reversible strain; do not melt; e.g. natural rubber (2 marks)
Only thermoplastics can be remelted because cross-links in the other two prevent the chains from flowing (2 marks)
questions.explanation: The key difference is the presence and density of cross-links. Thermoplastics have none and soften when heated, thermosets have many and become rigid networks, and elastomers have a few and stay rubbery.

questions.stem: A snap-fit clip in a car interior must work at 80 degrees C. Candidate A is an amorphous polymer with Tg of about 105 degrees C and candidate B has Tg of about 150 degrees C. Describe how the modulus of an amorphous polymer varies with temperature relative to Tg and explain which candidate is preferable at 80 degrees C, giving two further considerations for a snap-fit.
markingGuide: Below Tg: glassy plateau, modulus of the order of GPa (1 mark)
Around Tg: modulus falls by about three orders of magnitude (leathery region) (2 marks)
Above Tg: rubbery plateau of order MPa, then viscous flow if not cross-linked (1 mark)
At 80 degrees C, A is within about 25 degrees C of Tg, so it is softening and prone to creep and stress relaxation; B is well below Tg and retains its stiffness (2 marks)
Further considerations: creep or stress relaxation under the constant assembly strain; allowable strain and toughness (impact, fatigue) of the polymer (2 marks)
questions.explanation: Stiffness falls sharply near and above the glass transition, so a polymer should be used well below its Tg for load-bearing parts. Candidate B, with its much higher Tg, is better at 80 degrees C, and designers must also check creep and strain limits.
